parts.part: citadel (walled enclosure between two natural ridges)
parts.layout_phase: Phase 2 of Dales's sequence in Operation A-A/1 (Levels 10A, 10, 9 and 8)
parts.what_was_built: Two massive stone walls join the ends of two sandstone ridges and so enclose a raised plateau; Stein describes the larger wall as built of large, roughly squared slabs with little clay between the courses, about 30 feet thick at the base and 20 to 25 feet high as preserved, and a gate with the massive foundations of what may have been two towers at one corner of the enclosure (stein1931gedrosia pp. 61-62). Dales's L-shaped trench against the inner face of one wall reached natural soil and showed a solid mudbrick structure 2.3 m wide, built on a deliberate foundation of crushed stones and sand laid on the natural surface, against the inner face of the stone wall: 'a rampart, or better still, a "banquette"' (dales1992makran p. 137). He reconstructs seven phases, of which Phase 2 comprises 'Level 10A: foundation laid for the citadel enclosure. Level 10: construction of stone citadel wall and mudbrick rampart. Levels 9 and 8: earliest occupations associated with the citadel enclosure' (p. 138). Inside, stone house walls associated exclusively with Harappan sherds belong to later phases (pp. 135-136, 139).
parts.excavator_basis: Neither excavator gives an absolute date for the enclosure, and no radiocarbon sample has been published. Stein assigned the site to 'chalcolithic times' by comparing its surface finds, house contents and cinerary pots with sites in northern Baluchistan, and saw in the finds 'a single if prolonged period of occupation' (stein1931gedrosia pp. 63, 68). Dales identified the walled citadel as Harappan from the associated pottery and placed the Indus civilization in general at 'cir. 2500-1800 B.C.' (dales1992makran, Preface, pdf p. 11).

syntheses.statement: Dales, introducing Balakot as 'one of four known ancient coastal sites in Pakistan dating to the period of South Asia's earliest civilization-the Harappan (or Indus)-that flourished in the centuries just before and after 2000 B.C.', names Sutkagen Dor and Sotkha Koh as the two major sites found by the 1959-60 Makran survey.
syntheses.disagreement: Later and narrower than the 'cir. 2500-1800 B.C.' Dales gives in the 1992 report; neither is specific to Sutkagen-dor.

syntheses.statement: The Allchins mention Stein's trial trenches and add that 'More recently Dales has shown the existence of a great fortification around this Harappan outpost.'

The Pakistan Department of Archaeology and Museums heritage database gives 'Relative Chronology: 3500 BCE - 1800 BCE' and says 'The pottery represented Kulli-Harappan cultures', citing Possehl, The Indus Age: The Beginnings (1999).
syntheses.disagreement: Begins a millennium earlier than any Harappan date; it is a relative span for the whole site from a heritage inventory, not a dated layout.

parts.conflicts: No source dates the citadel wall. The published statements are general spans for the Harappan or Indus period: 'the centuries just before and after 2000 B.C.' (Dales 1977), 'cir. 2500-1800 B.C.' (Dales 1992) and 3500-1800 BCE (Pakistan heritage database). Dales notes that his seven-phase reading of Trench A-A/1 differs in 'a couple minor discrepancies' from the version Mughal submitted to the Department of Archaeology (p. 138).

first_occupation.phase: Phase 1 of Dales's sequence (Level 11): 'the earliest presence of the Harappans who presumably brought with them micaceous pottery from Sind'
first_occupation.basis: Stratigraphic: Level 11 lies on wash over the natural surface (Level 12) and below the foundation of the enclosure (Level 10A); no date is given.

notes: Sutkagen-dor is the westernmost Harappan site, on the Dasht river in Makran, and its layout is a fortified enclosure rather than a street grid: stone walls with a gateway close the gaps between two rocky ridges, and a mudbrick rampart stands against the inner face of the wall. Dales's 1960 test trench showed that the enclosure was founded in his Phase 2, directly after a thin first Harappan occupation (Phase 1) on the natural surface, so layout and first occupation are close in time. The site has no published radiocarbon date and no excavator's absolute date, so every date field is empty and the syntheses give only general spans. Dales's soundings in the 'lower town' east of the citadel went 4.5 to 5 m down through sterile silt and found no occupation strata, so we record no lower-town part (dales1992makran pp. 44, 46, 139). We read Stein's 1931 report and the full 1992 report of Dales's survey; Dales's preliminary article 'Harappan outposts on the Makran coast' (Antiquity 36, 1962: 86-92) is paywalled on Cambridge Core and was not read, and Possehl's compilations were not available. The Antiquity abstract page we fetched carried no dating information and was not kept. Directions and bearings of the walls given by Stein and Dales are deliberately not recorded.
